title: When the Van Breaks Down
subtitle: Stars Between the Strings · Chapter 16 of 40
content:
The van broke down again in front of the bakery, which Greg claimed was an improvement because at least the pastries were nearby.

The engine made one sharp cough and went silent. Greg turned the key twice more. Nothing happened.

“It’s thinking,” he said.

“It’s dead.”

“It’s considering its options.”

“It has chosen death.”

Greg rested his head against the steering wheel. “The van has a flair for drama.”

I climbed out and opened the hood. The belt looked worse than it had on the cow road. A dark stain spread beneath the engine.

“You said the last repair was mostly compatible.”

“It was compatible with optimism.”

“That is not a mechanical category.”

“It should be.”

The mechanic quoted Greg a price that made his shoulders tense. The van needed more than a belt. It needed patience, money, and a part that had not been manufactured in this century.

“We can sell it,” Greg said afterward.

I stood beside him on the sidewalk. “You don’t want to.”

“No.”

“Then don’t.”

“It’s expensive.”

“So is every object you love.”

He gave me a wounded look.

“That was affectionate,” I said.

“I’m not sure my wallet understands affection.”

The mechanic offered them a temporary ride. Greg declined. He called a friend instead, and the two of us walked to the car wash while waiting.

“I can pay for part of the repair,” I said.

Greg stopped. “No.”

“You didn’t let me finish.”

“I know where this is going.”

“You don’t.”

“I know I love you, and I know I don’t want you feeling responsible for keeping my life intact.”

“I’m not responsible for your life. I’m your partner.”

The word stopped him.

“Partner,” he repeated.

“Is that wrong?”

“No.” He looked down at the pavement. “It’s just bigger than girlfriend or boyfriend.”

“We’re bigger than a label.”

“That’s a very romantic thing to say.”

“I’m a romantic.”

“You learned from me.”

“I’m improving on the source material.”

He laughed, but the worry returned.

“I want to help,” I said. “Not because I’m obligated. Because I choose you.”

“You could use the money for your studio.”

“I can do both.”

“What if this is the start of you carrying me?”

“Then we talk before it becomes that.”

Greg looked at me for a long moment. “You make partnership sound like a conversation instead of a trap.”

“It is a conversation.”

“I’m not used to that.”

“Then we can practice.”

I paid for half the repair. Greg argued. I argued better. The mechanic agreed that my argument had structural integrity and accepted the money.

While the van was in the shop, Greg stayed with me in the studio. The room felt smaller with both of us inside it, but not in a bad way. He cooked pasta in the kitchenette. I sat on the counter and read the instructions aloud even though he did not need them.

“The sauce says simmer,” I said.

“I know what simmer means.”

“Do you?”

“I have met a pot before.”

“Your van would disagree.”

He stirred the sauce. I watched the line of his shoulders, the way he moved around the kitchen without assuming which cabinets belonged to him.

“What?” he asked.

“Nothing.”

“You’re doing the face.”

“I’m thinking.”

“Dangerous.”

“How do you know when a place is yours?”

Greg turned off the burner.

“That’s a big question for pasta.”

“The pasta can handle it.”

He leaned against the counter. “Maybe when you stop measuring how much of yourself you’re allowed to leave there.”

I looked around the studio. My books rested on the shelf. My clothes hung in the closet. Greg's guitar pick sat in the dish beside my keys.

“I’m still measuring,” I said.

“I know.”

“I don’t want to.”

“Then leave something.”

“What?”

“Anything.”

I considered the room. Then I took the small framed photograph from my bag. It showed a place I had once called home, before the word became complicated.

I placed it on the shelf beside the records.

Greg did not ask who was in it.

“That’s important,” he said.

“It’s a memory.”

“Those can be important.”

I stepped closer. “What did you leave in the van?”

“Several scarves, a pick, two books, and my heart.”

“Your heart is not an object.”

“It is when I’m writing a song.”

“What song?”

He touched my photograph, then looked at me. “The one about staying.”

The kiss began softly. Greg's hand found my waist. I leaned into him, and the kitchen filled with the scent of tomato and basil.

“The pasta,” I whispered.

“It has had a good life.”

“Greg.”

He turned off the lights. “I’ll save it.”

The door closed between the kitchen and the rest of the world. Dinner waited. The van waited. The future waited.

For a while, I did not.

The next afternoon, the van returned with a new belt, a repaired hose, and a receipt that made Greg physically ill.

He started the engine. It purred.

“It lives,” he said.

“It has chosen a temporary reprieve.”

“You’re learning.”

He drove to the beach. I sat beside him, my hand in his.

“Thank you,” he said.

“For paying for the van?”

“For arguing with me.”

“That’s free.”

“It’s not.”

He parked near the boardwalk and turned to me.

“I don’t want to be saved,” he said. “But I do want to be helped.”

I nodded. “Those are different.”

“I’m learning.”

“We both are.”

Greg kissed my hand. “Partner?”

“Partner.”

The van carried me home, one repaired part at a time.

The next week, the mechanic called to say the replacement part had failed.

Greg stared at the phone. “It has betrayed me.”

“It was compatible with optimism,” I reminded him.

“You are enjoying this.”

“A little.”

He sat on the edge of the new couch in my apartment. The van was parked outside, silent and expensive. the two of us had spent the afternoon listing possible repairs, costs, and alternatives.

“We could sell it,” Greg said.

“You could.”

“I don’t want to.”

“Then repair it.”

“What if repairing it is irresponsible?”

“Then decide what the van is worth to you.”

“You make it sound easy.”

“It’s not easy. It’s just a choice.”

Greg looked down at his hands. “I’m afraid that if I let it go, I’ll lose the last proof that I am still the person who drove away.”

“Do you want to be that person?”

“Sometimes.”

“Why?”

“Because he did not need anyone.”

The answer was so sad that I moved closer.

“He also had nowhere to come back to,” I said.

Greg's eyes lifted.

“You don’t have to keep the van to prove you survived,” I continued. “You can keep it because you love it. Or let it go because you are allowed to become someone new.”

He leaned into my shoulder.

“I hate when you are right,” he murmured.

“I am very difficult to argue with.”

“You are very easy to love.”

The words softened the room.

The van was repaired again. Not because it was the only home Greg had, but because it was part of a life he still wanted. He painted the repaired shelf blue. He added my name to a small list of emergency contacts. He put a second blanket in the back.

“For lumbar support?” I asked.

“For emotional lumbar support.”

“Of course.”

I took him by the hand and kissed him in the open van door.

The city moved around me. The road remained available. The difference was that Greg no longer needed to run every time he felt afraid.

Neither did I.

At the car wash, Greg played a new song about repairs. The chorus compared a broken belt to a wounded heart. Mara threw a towel at him.

“Too obvious,” she said.

“People like obvious.”

“People like working brakes.”

I laughed from the front row. Greg looked at me while he sang the final verse.

Afterward, he asked whether the song was terrible.

“It is sincere.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is a kind answer.”

“I’ll take it.”

He kissed me beside the soap dispensers.

“That was a terrible song,” Mara called.

“You listened to the whole thing,” Greg replied.

“I was trapped by the chorus.”

I smiled at him. “She is jealous of the bridge.”

“Everyone is jealous of the bridge.”

“The bridge is innocent.”

“The bridge knows what it did.”

He took my hand as the car wash lights came on. The van waited at the curb, repaired and stubborn. We walked home together instead.

The road could wait until tomorrow.

At home, Greg wrote the repair date on the calendar. I circled it twice and added a note: BRING SNACKS.

He added: BRING MORE SNACKS.

The plan was sound.

Especially the snacks.

Greg circled the date in blue ink. I added a small star beside it. Neither of us pretended the appointment was more important than the relationship, but both of us intended to keep it.

The calendar was enough.

I kept the appointment.
